houston-houston-1915-08.A2:
TROOPERS SAVE BLACK
State Gets Help of Government in Conducting Negro to Trial-Guard Is Sixty Strong
HOUSTON, Tex., Aug. 9.—Sixty state troopers, infantry and cavalry, under command of Captain Dallas J. Matthews, left Houston this morning with Sam Jernagan, negro, who will be placed on trial at Groverton, Tex., on a charge of criminal assault on a white woman. This measure of protection was taken on the advice of the Trinity county sheriff, who had sent Jernagan to the Harris county jail for safe keeping.
houston-houston-1915-08.A4:
[By Associated Press.]

Houston, Tex., Aug. 12.—Sam Jernagan, a negro, today was given the death penalty at Groveton, the jury finding him guilty of criminal assault upon Rosa Vondra, a fourteen-year-old white girl. The conviction was obtained on Jernagan's confession. The negro did not take the stand and accepted the verdict stolidly. State troops guarded the prisoner while being taken from Houston to Groveton and during the trial.

Now the trial of the prisoner is set in the county where the crime was committed. The sheriff, realizing the danger of violence, requested of the governor military protection for the prisoner during the trial, and it was immediately given.

If this negro is guilty, he will be convicted by the due process of law and executed, and the execution of a brave and efficient sheriff will be stainless, and the reputation of a good old county inhabited by good people, will be saved the disgrace of a lynching.

It may be that Sheriff Thornton will be held in reprobation because of his efforts to save his prisoner, which it was his sworn duty to do, but not by cool-headed people who realize the folly of mob law.

We commend Sheriff Thornton's whole course because, if all sheriffs would follow his example the curse of mob law would soon be stamped out in the South. The great majority of lynchings could be prevented if the officers would, in all cases of arrest of negroes charged with outrageous crimes, remember their sworn duty and exhaust every resource at their command to prevent mob violence.

Duty is the noblest word in the language for a sheriff, for it embraces everything that establishes his qualifications for office.—Houston Post.
houston-houston-1915-08.A10:
A GOOD EXAMPLE.
Sheriff Thornton of Trinity county deserves commendation as a conscientious officer, one who does his duty without regard to the feelings of others, and one who does not let any consideration of how his acts may affect his political life stand in the way of the proper performance of his duty.

Some time ago a negro was arrested on a charge of having committed a nameless crime against a white girl. Despite the attempts of a mob to lynch the prisoner, Sheriff Thornton took him toward Houston, the negro escaping en route. He was recaptured the same night, taken to Houston and lodged in jail.

When the time for his trial in Groveton arrived, the prisoner was taken under escort of state troops to that town and was tried, convicted and sentenced to the death penalty, the soldiers guarding the courthouse during the trial. As the Galveston News says, the sheriff may have alienated, at least for the time, some of his friends, "but that will count for little against the satisfaction that must come to him from the consciousness that his offense was in being true to his oath." There have been cases where an of-

ficer of the law, either for expediency or from cowardice, has submitted to the mob and surrendered his prisoner, perhaps feeling that the prisoners was getting no more than his just deserts.

But a true officer of the law, one who is determined to live up to the oath of office which he took, will resist to the extent of his ability any attempt of unauthorized persons to take a prisoner away from him. He is not the judge of the man's guilt, nor the one to assess his punishment. His duty consists in safeguarding the prisoner for the due process of law, regardless of how his attitude may affect others.

And even the lower and less responsible elements which enter into a mob cannot help respecting and admiring an officer who does his duty, even risking his life—not to save the prisoner, but to defend the majesty of the law.

As the years roll on there are less of the mob crimes reported, and it is evident that the people are more law-abiding and more willing to let the law take its course than in the past.

There is little reason for anyone to fear that a brute accused of such a crime will escape through technicalities or subterfuges. It is, indeed, becoming difficult to find a lawyer who will accept the defense of such a case, and usually the court has to appoint one.

Then, again, the negroes as a whole do not now attempt to save one of their race who is accused of such a crime. There have been many cases in recent years where the negroes turned out to aid the white people in prehending a negro accused of assault upon a white woman, and the guilty fugitive can no longer look to his people to hide him or aid in his escape.

For these reasons, there is no excuse for the lynching of a man accused of such a crime. Only the brutality which comes to the surface when such an outrage is perpetrated causes the assembling of the mob, and the veneer of civilization is thrown off to expose the savage underneath.

It is a pleasure to record the bravery, physical as well as moral, of such a man as Sheriff Thornton, and we are sure that when his fellow citizens take cool counsel they will thank him for protecting them against themselves, and preventing the perpetration of an outrage which would have cast discredit upon their community.

Nafarrete denies that his men crossed into Texas, and cites as proof that he has only 500 men from Los Aldamas to the mouth of the river. But what became of the 2,000 more which he claimed a week ago to have?

A quiet night was reported from the Brownsville section, only three bandits having been killed. It takes more than that down there to be considered as a disturbance.

If those invaders were not Carranza troops, how does it happen that they abandoned a lot of Mauser rifles like the Carrancistas use? One cannot buy that kind of arms in this country, and no one in that section is importing them from Europe.

Chicago is to have a municipal wood yard where unemployed men will be given a dollar a day. This is to prevent the I Won't Workers from securing lodging in the municipal rooming houses. But as soon as they get a dollar or two they can sleep in the box cars and eat free lunch.

The death toll in the Brownsville section amounts to about twenty. Anywhere else this would be considered awful, but down there it is only a little more than usual, and excites little comment.

Calls Militia to Groveton.
Houston, Tex.—Thirty men of the Houston Cavalry, Texas National Guard, commanded by Captain Roy Blount, and thirty men of the Houston Light Guard, commanded by Captain Dallas Matthews, left Sunday for Groveton, Trinity county, to assist the sheriff of that county in protecting the negro, Jernagan, who is being tried at Groveton this week week on a charge of criminal assault.

john-salter-evergreen-1915-08-06.A2:
FOUR HANG IN ALABAMA.
Governor Refuses to Interfere, So Murderers Die.
MONTGOMERY, Ala., August 6.—Four persons were legally executed in Alabama today. Gov. Henderson refusing to reprieve in all cases.

At Evergreen Robert Watkins and John Salter, negroes, were hanged while a squad of militiamen stood guard. The negroes murdered Mrs. Mary Lasseter, a white woman; left Wiley House, a planter, for dead, and burned the farmhouse.

At Cullman George James, white, was hanged for the murder in Decatur of George Clayburn. James shot Clayburn through an open window while the latter was reading his Bible at night.

Millard Carpenter, a negro, was hanged at Birmingham for the murder two years ago of John T. Camp, a transfer man.
john-salter-evergreen-1915-08-06.A4:
TWO NEGROES HANGED FOR LASSITER MURDER Both Confessed Their Crime—Each Died With a Smile On His Lips. Special to The Advertiser.
EVERGREEN, ALA., Aug. 6.—Two negroes, John Salter and Robert Watkins, were hanged here today shortly after 11 o'clock. The Watkins negro went on the gallows first and was pronounced dead in eight minutes. Salter's death was almost instantaneous with the drop.

Both negroes showed remarkable nerve. They had shown little or no concern over their approaching doom since their conviction and sentence to death, and today when they mounted the scaffold each one did so with a smile on his face, and talked to the assembled crowd until the cap was adjusted.

The crime for which the two were executed was the brutal murder of Martha Lassiter, some twelve miles north of here, on the night of June 23rd. They were arrested the following day, confessed their crime and were convicted at a special term of Circuit court two weeks later and sentenced to be hanged today.

Sheriff Williams carried out the execution without a hitch. More than two thousand people came to town today, but only a few were permitted to witness the execution.

john-salter-evergreen-1915-08-06.A5:
Women See Executions and Crowd Sings Hymn-One Slayer Pursued.
MEMPHIS, Aug. 7.—Nine negroes were hanged, seven legally and two lynched, yesterday, in the southern states, while a tenth is being chased near Liberty, Mo., by a lynching party.

Alabama led the list with four legal hangings. The governor refused reprieves in each case. At Evergreen, Robert Watkins and John Salter were hanged while a squad of militiamen stood guard to prevent disorder, threatened by citizens who wanted the blacks burned for the murder and assault of Mrs. Mary Lassiter at Cullman.

George James was hanged for the murder of George Clayburn, who was shot through an open window while he was reading a Bible. Millard Carpenter was hanged at Birmingham for the murder two years ago of John T. Camp, a white man.

WOMEN ATTEND HANGING.

Mississippi hanged three negroes, but with two of them, Peter Bolen and Jim Seales, convicted of murdering another negro, an unusual spectacle was made. The hanging was at Fresco, the gallows being erected between two beautiful hills in a natural amphitheater.

Many women were in the crowd of 5,000 people and excursions were run from nearby towns. Just as the traps were sprung simultaneously the crowd burst forth into the hymn, "There Is a Land of Pure Delight," at the request of the negroes just before death.

Bunyan Walters was hanged at Fayetteville, Miss., for the murder of Tom Neals.

AN "ORDERLY MOB."

Dispatches from Shawnee, Okla., tell of a "quiet, orderly crowd armed to the teeth," which hanged Ed Berry to a Santa Fe railroad bridge, riddled his body with bullets and dispersed in as orderly a fashion as it had formed.

In the early morning hours at Trilby, Fla., a crowd, hypnotized with fury, lynched Will Leach, accused of attacking a 13-year-old girl.

At last reports a mob of 500 men were closing in on a negro near Liberty, Mo., who attacked a farmer's wife. Lynching is almost certain, it is said.
john-salter-evergreen-1915-08-06.A16:
THE JONES AUTO THROUGH THE EAST.
Mr. and Mrs. Abel L. Jones, 2009 Colafax street, Evanston, have left for the East on an auto tour. They will stop at Toledo, O., Sandusky, Cleveland, and Pittsburgh, Pa., and will return to stop over at the Knights of Pythias in the cement at Columbus, O. They intend to be gone about three weeks.
